Chapter 4: Feminism, Capitalism, and the Commodification of Empowerment
Everywhere you look these days, you’ll find the language of empowerment. It’s woven into ads, splashed across social media, and baked right into those catchy corporate mission statements. Promises of strength, independence, and self-love seem to be everywhere. At first glance, it almost feels like a win—like feminism has finally made it to the mainstream. But, if you look a little closer, you’ll notice there’s something more complicated going on under those shiny slogans.
Picture this: a young woman is walking through a busy shopping mall, surrounded by billboards and window displays urging her to “be herself,” “love her body,” and “break the rules.” Every product—whether it’s makeup, clothes, or the latest fitness class—is sold as a tool of liberation, a way to show off confidence and individuality. The message? That empowerment is just a purchase away. That self-worth can be found at the checkout counter.
It’s easy to see why this version of feminism is so tempting. It feels good. It promises agency, control, and a chance to break free from old limitations. But here’s where it gets tricky: it turns empowerment into just another thing to buy. Instead of something we live and breathe, it becomes something we consume. The spotlight shifts—from collective change to personal achievement, from transforming the world to simply transforming ourselves.
Take the rise of “girlboss” culture. It’s this idea that women can succeed entirely on their own terms, that they can truly have it all if they just work hard enough. On one hand, it’s inspiring. On the other? It’s exhausting. There’s this constant pressure to be productive, attractive, and absolutely self-assured. Suddenly, the language of empowerment isn’t freeing—it’s one more expectation to meet. One more way to measure whether you’re winning or falling behind.
For a lot of people, the promise of empowerment bumps up against the grind of daily life. The wage gap, workplace discrimination, and unpaid labor—they’re all still very real. When we focus so much on individual achievement, it’s easy to lose sight of these big, structural barriers. That “anything is possible” message? It can start to sound a little hollow when you’re up against systems that just aren’t fair.
And it’s not just advertising. This commodification of feminism slips into every part of our culture. It shapes how we talk about relationships, work, and even self-care. The idea that buying the right product or changing your mindset can fix really deep issues is comforting, sure. But it’s also misleading. It shifts the weight off society, putting it all on the individual—and that makes it so much harder to see why we need to come together and push for real change.
Most folks don’t realize just how easily empowerment language gets swept up by capitalism. The line between genuine progress and empty marketing? It can be really blurry. Wanting to feel strong and independent is totally real—but the quick fixes we’re sold are often just surface-level. When all the focus is on personal transformation, it’s tough to notice how much the system itself needs to change.
Over time, you start to see that true empowerment can’t be bought or sold. It takes a willingness to question the stories we’re told—about ourselves, about the world. It means knowing there are limits to what we can do alone, and that solidarity really matters. The language of empowerment is powerful, no doubt. But it only means something when it’s tied to real, lasting change.
